claims.text: Elemental Cr coatings on zirconium-alloy cladding suffer Cr–Zr interdiffusion at elevated temperatures.
Elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion causes premature failure of the baseline elemental Cr coating.
A CrN interlayer between the zirconium-alloy substrate and elemental Cr coating will mitigate high-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
The proposed CrN interlayer would be tens of nanometers thick and deposited by a controlled vapor-deposition process.
The CrN interlayer will remain continuous, adherent, chemically stable, and intact during service.
An intact CrN interlayer will physically and chemically impede migration of Zr atoms into the Cr coating.
CrN has sufficiently high thermal stability to function as an interdiffusion barrier in the proposed service environments.
Zr has low diffusivity in the CrN structure.
At normal operating temperatures, the CrN barrier will preserve the corrosion-resistant character of the elemental Cr coating.
Under high-temperature steam, the CrN barrier will prevent premature interdiffusion-driven degradation and coating failure.
Normal subcritical-water operation is represented by exposure at approximately 300–350°C.
Accident-relevant conditions are represented by short transient steam exposure at temperatures up to approximately 1200°C.
Relative to the unmodified Cr-coated baseline, the CrN-modified system will exhibit markedly reduced Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Relative to the baseline, the CrN-modified system will have enhanced coating longevity.
The CrN-modified system will provide performance comparable to the baseline under normal operation.
The CrN-modified system will be significantly superior to the baseline in resisting diffusion-induced degradation during high-temperature steam exposure.
The long-term thermal and chemical stability of the CrN barrier under cyclic thermal stress remains unverified.
The optimal CrN thickness and deposition parameters needed to maximize barrier performance without compromising adhesion are not determined.
